sub_answers.text: He was first elected to the State Legislature from Chalakurthi in 1983.[d21669170s1p0] He was re-elected seven times to the Assembly from the Chalakurthi constituency.[d21669170s1p0] He held multiple state cabinet portfolios including Agriculture, Co-operative, Marketing, Forest, Animal Husbandry, Fisheries, Weights & Measures, C.A.D., Transport, Roads & Buildings, Housing, Panchayath Raj, Rural water scheme and Sanitation in the government of Andhra Pradesh (dates not individually specified in the chunks).[d21669170s1p0] He was sworn in as Minister for Home Affairs in the 2004 Andhra Pradesh cabinet and served as Minister for Home, Jails, Fire Service, Sainik Welfare, Printing & Stationery from 2004 to 2009.[d21669170s1p0][d21669170s0p0] He served as Minister for Panchayat Raj & Rural Water Supply in Andhra Pradesh from 2009 to 2014.[d21669170s0p0]

sub_answers.text: He won the 2009 election with a margin of 6,214 votes against Chinappa Reddy Tera.[d21669170s0p0] He won the 2014 election with a margin of 16,558 votes over Nomula Narsimaiah of BRS.[d21669170s0p0] He lost the 1994 election to TDP candidate Gundeboina Rammoorthy Yadav.[d21669170s0p0] He was first elected in 1983 and was re-elected seven times from the Chalakurthi constituency (individual vote counts or overall vote shares are not provided in the chunks).[d21669170s1p0]

sub_answers.text: He was appointed as the first Chairman of the Telangana Sahitya Akademi, an academy established to ensure regular research, analysis, publishing and propagation of the Telugu language [d64548874s3p0]. He was a member of a committee to review Telugu language textbooks addressing dialect and style issues [d64548874s3p0]. He headed a Telangana state government committee on the syllabus for recruitment exams to replace the old Andhra Pradesh–drafted syllabus with a Telangana‑centric syllabus [d64548874s3p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List and summarize major public scandals, allegations of bribery, misuse of office, or financial irregularities linked to the Congress leader (or their close aides/family); for each, cite the primary evidence reported (documents, audits, whistleblower testimony, media investigations) and any official admissions or denials.

Identify criminal or civil cases, anti-corruption agency investigations, election petitions, or appellate court judgments that were filed against the leader or policies they championed; for each case provide the charges, courts or agencies involved, key legal findings, and final disposition or current status.

Gather documented critiques from opposition parties, prominent NGOs, activist groups, and editorial investigations about the leader’s policy decisions and administrative style; specify the exact policy or action criticized, the evidence or examples cited by critics, and any independent fact-checks or rebuttals.

Describe the formal institutional, statutory, or constitutional limits (e.g., federal/state division of powers, party caucus rules, legislative majorities, judicial review, bureaucratic constraints) that constrained the leader’s ability to enact policies, with concrete examples of when those constraints blocked or diluted specific initiatives.

During the leader's term, how did quantifiable administrative performance metrics—such as average processing time for citizen services, percentage of digitized state services, audit findings, and compliance rates with statutory service standards—evolve compared to the prior administration?

Which specific policy areas saw budget reallocations or new flagship programs under the leader (for example changes in health-care spending per capita, school enrollment targets, kilometers of roads/rail funded, expansion of cash-transfer or pension schemes), and how did official planning documents and legislative agendas reflect those priority shifts?

What were the state-level economic indicators (annual real GDP growth, unemployment/underemployment rates, formal sector job creation, investment inflows, fiscal balance or credit ratings) during each year of the leader's tenure, and how do those figures compare with the five-year period immediately before they took office?

How did systematic measures of public sentiment—polling approval ratings, trust-in-government surveys, electoral performance in midterm/local contests, and social-media sentiment trends—change from the start to the end of the leader's term, including major inflection points and underlying demographic breakdowns if available?

Provide a chronological list of every state-level election the Congress leader contested (assembly and by-elections), showing the year, constituency, opponent(s), vote counts and percentage share for the leader and the nearest competitor, and the margin of victory or defeat.

List specific administrative reorganizations the Congress party chief introduced within the state civil service: name the departments merged, split, or abolished; the dates each change was announced and took effect; the notifications or gazette publications that formalized them; and the stated rationale for each move.

Identify the exact legal tools the leader used to implement policy shifts at the state level — cite ordinance numbers, executive order titles, cabinet decisions, amendments to state acts, or specific bills tabled in the assembly — including dates of issuance, the ministries that issued them, and any enabling clauses relied upon.

Describe alterations the leader made to public expenditure priorities: provide comparative budget line items (pre- and post-change), the fiscal years impacted, new flagship programs funded or defunded, any revised budget rules or approval procedures introduced, and references to budget speeches, finance department orders, or audit notes documenting the changes.

Specify which new bodies (commissions, statutory authorities, ad hoc task forces, oversight cells) the leader created or granted expanded powers: give their legal basis or government order numbers, membership and chair appointments, mandates and lifespan, the administrative or financial powers delegated, and examples of decisions or reports they produced.

Detail the principal controversies, bribery or corruption allegations, ethics inquiries, or scandal narratives associated with the Congress leader; cite documented incidents, dates, accused associates, media investigations, official findings, and primary source evidence.

List the criminal suits, public interest litigations, commission or agency investigations, appellate or supreme court rulings, and parliamentary probe reports that were filed against the leader or policies they championed; summarize charges, legal basis, procedural history, verdicts or ongoing status, and any penalties or injunctions imposed.

Catalog the substantive critiques leveled by rival political parties, advocacy groups, watchdog NGOs, investigative journalists, and human rights organizations concerning the leader’s policy choices and management style; include specific policy decisions criticized, supporting statements or reports, and documented examples of governance failures or rights concerns.

Identify the formal institutional, statutory, or constitutional limits—such as federal/state divisions, legislative majorities, judicial review powers, administrative rules, budgetary constraints, or party discipline—that constrained the leader’s capacity to enact their program; provide examples of attempts thwarted or modified by these limits and references to the controlling legal or procedural provisions.

Across the leader’s time in office, how did official indicators of state administrative performance—such as average permit processing times, complaint resolution rates, audit compliance scores, and civil service vacancy/turnover figures—trend year by year?

During the administration, which specific policy initiatives or budgetary reallocations show a documented shift in priorities (for example changes in ministerial budget shares, new flagship programs, legislative acts, or targets in public health, school enrollment/learning metrics, road/kilometre targets, and social protection caseloads)?
sub_answers.text: A committee including Nandini Sidda Reddy reviewed whether Telugu textbooks should use the spoken Telangana dialect or the traditional Sanskritised Telugu in 2014–2015 [d64548874s3p0]. [d64548874s3p0] The old syllabus for recruitment exams drafted by the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission was replaced by a Telangana‑centric new syllabus via a state government committee on which he served in 2015 [d64548874s3p0]. [d64548874s0p0] He was appointed the first Chairman of the Telangana Sahitya Akademi on 2 May 2017, an institution established to support research, publishing and propagation of the Telugu language, and he remained Chairman as of 2020 [d64548874s3p0] [d64548874s0p0]. [d64548874s3p0] The Telangana Sahitya Akademi under his chairmanship headed the World Telugu Conference held in Hyderabad from 15–19 December 2017, a major cultural flagship event [d64548874s3p0].

What do available time-series measures of public sentiment show over the leader’s tenure—for example longitudinal approval-rating polls, trust-in-government surveys, election vote shares or midterm referendum results, and major opinion-poll breakpoints—and how did these metrics change at key events during their governance?
sub_answers.text: In the 2014 elections the Congress won 21 out of 119 seats in Telangana and suffered heavy losses compared with 2009, marking a major low point for the party in the state [d42183620s1p0]. [d42183620s1p0] In the 2018 Telangana Legislative Assembly elections the Congress, as part of the Praja Kutami alliance, won 19 seats (the alliance won 21 seats total and about 33% of the vote) while TRS increased its majority [d42183620s1p0]. [d42183620s1p0] In the 2020 Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation elections Congress won only 2 seats, prompting the state president N. Uttam Kumar Reddy to resign and later leading to Revanth Reddy's appointment as state party chief in 2021 [d42183620s1p0]. [d42183620s1p0] In the 2023 Telangana Legislative Assembly election the Congress won the state for the first time, a result widely credited to PCC Chief Revanth Reddy and a wave of anti‑incumbency and rural dissatisfaction [d42183620s1p0]. [d42183620s1p0] In the 2024 Indian general election the Congress won 8 seats in Telangana with a 40.10% vote share [d42183620s1p0].
